addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: amortized + cached calibration**

Framing is measured un-amortized, so it inherits the full
~10 ns TSC quantum (run-to-run reports span 0-21 ns on the
3900X; cold runs on r5-7600x clamp to 0.00) and the estimate
sizes `inner`, so a low draw under-sizes the experiment (up to
~9% relative error, worst case ~50% apparatus contamination).
Fix per
[analysis](design.md#calibration-accuracy-framing-quantization),
revised mid-cycle by the in-interval vs call-to-call finding
([analysis](design.md#timer-overhead-in-interval-vs-call-to-call)):
amortized two-point window calibration (error q/M on both
points) yields `frame_call_ns` (sizes `inner`; never
subtracted) and `loop_per_iter_ns` (the only subtraction);
cache the constants in the config file with provenance + a
live validity check, and say cached vs live in the report
header. Calibration banner values print at 3 decimals always
(sub-ns resolution is the point; `--decimals` remains the
report-table knob). The -2 experiment precedes the cache steps
because its outcome decides which constants the cache stores:
if the dithered mean-based fit's intercept is stable
run-to-run
([analysis](design.md#dithering-random-phase-injection)), it
*becomes* the calibration — loop/iter and in-interval framing
with per-block CIs (subtraction returns), plus one window pass
for the call-to-call sizing constant. -3 also dithers the
harness sample seam (Bench-driven benches only: a run's
aggregate means stop carrying the coherent ±q phase bias,
~±2% on fast benches; a seam delay inside a probe bench's
closed loop would perturb what's measured, so that stays a
separate opt-in idea). -4 pulls "Within-invocation
replication: sleep-separated blocks" forward
([analysis](design.md#within-invocation-replication-sleep-separated-blocks)):
`--blocks N` splits a run into N sleep-separated blocks
(random-ms sleep + unrecorded post-wake warm-up per block),
reports block mean ± 95% CI and the LSC, Bench-driven benches
only; ANOVA validation (between-block vs between-invocation)
on r5-7600x decides how honest the single-run CI is.

- 0.21.0-2 feat: dithered calibration experiment (done)

content.content:
auto-sized bench.
- Under-estimated framing under-sizes `inner`: a 1.02 ns
  calibration draw on a ~2.9 ns step picks inner ≈ 4 instead
  of ~43; the true ~11 ns framing is then ~2.8 ns per call
  (~50% apparatus), of which only 0.26 ns is subtracted.
  Nothing in the report reveals it.
- `--inner` override at 1 exposes the full δ (~10-20 ns)
  per call, unamortized.

Consequence: a min-of-mins repeat of the current fit would
be the wrong fix — consistently landing on the *low* quantum
consistently under-sizes `inner`. Over-estimating framing is
harmless (bigger `inner`); under-estimating distorts.

### Fix: amortized framing measurement

Measure the timer-pair cost inside one window: one timer
read at the start, a loop of M back-to-back timer pairs, one
read at the end, divide by M. The ±1-quantum error on the
window amortizes to q/M per pair (~0.001 ns at M = 10,000) —
the same trick that already makes loop/iter steady.

Caveat: this measures the *throughput* cost of paired reads,
which can differ from a timer pair pipelined around real
work. We think it is still a far better subtraction constant
than "somewhere in a 10 ns interval", but it carries a
different (small) bias, not ground truth.

### Frequency dependence: what is constant, what is not

- The TSC rate and its ~10 ns quantum are invariant —
  constant across turbo, throttle, and idle states.
- The framing *cost* is core-clocked work (~tens of cycles
  of `rdtsc` + arithmetic), so its wall-clock value scales
  with core frequency: the same cycles take ~2× longer at a
  2.2 GHz throttle vs 4.6 GHz boost. Same for loop/iter.
- In practice calibration (post-warmup) and benches (hot
  loops) both run boosted, so the constants usually match.
  When frequency does shift, step cost shifts with framing
  cost, so contamination stays roughly proportional rather
  than blowing up; the subtraction just stops being exact.

So a cached calibration is a *machine + frequency-regime*
constant, not a universal one.

### Design: cached calibration in the config file

Store the calibration constants in the existing config file
(`src/config.rs`) rather than measuring fresh each run. The
primary benefit is run-to-run *comparability*, not startup
time: with a pinned adjustment constant, deltas between runs
reflect the bench, not the calibration lottery (~±0.23 ns on
adjusted values at inner = 43 today).

- An explicit calibrate command writes/refreshes the entry;
  runs use it when present, calibrate live otherwise.
- The entry carries provenance: CPU model, iiac-perf
  version, calibration date, raw `min_low`/`min_high`.
- Each run does a quick live amortized framing check
  (milliseconds) against the cached value: within a few
  percent, use the cache silently; off by more (throttle,
  different governor, stale file), warn or fall back to
  live. Cache validity becomes measured, not trusted.
- The report header states which mode adjusted the run —
  cached (with date) vs live — so a report is never
  ambiguous about its constants.

Rejected alternative: scaling calibration length with bench
duration (`-d` percentage). The residual error is
quantization, not sampling depth — more time in one
continuous measurement does not re-roll the phase alignment —
and calibration measures a machine property, not a bench
property.

## Timer overhead: in-interval vs call-to-call

Analysis from a 2026-07-13 session (3900X + r5-7600x),
prompted by implementing the amortized framing fix above: the
amortized measurement came out 5-10x larger than the intercept
fit it replaced (3900X: ~50 ns vs 1-21 ns; r5-7600x: ~23-32 ns
vs 0-4.5 ns). Both are "the cost of the timer pair" — they
measure different slices of it.

A sample is `now()` (clock read A) ... inner loop ...
`elapsed()` (clock read B); the recorded value is B - A. The
two timer calls cost ~23-50 ns in total, but most of that
sits *before read A* and *after read B* — outside the
recorded interval. Only a small sliver lands inside B - A.

- **In-interval overhead** (~1-11 ns) — the sliver: `now()`'s
  tail after read A, loop entry, `elapsed()`'s prologue up to
  read B; out-of-order execution overlaps much of it with the
  workload. This is what subtraction would want to remove
  from a sample.
- **Call-to-call overhead** (~23-50 ns) — the full apparatus
  cost of taking a sample, both clock-read latencies
  included. This is what throughput sees, and what sizing
  (`pick_inner`) and duration budgeting care about.

The measurability is asymmetric, and unfavorably so:

- Call-to-call amortizes: a window around M whole samples
  contains every bit of the pair cost, so q/M quantization →
  measured to ±0.02 ns warm (r5-7600x: 32.355 ns back-to-back
  pairs, identical across 5 runs; 23.07 ns in the two-point
  window shape, ±0.1%).
- In-interval cannot amortize *by construction*: any window
  wraps whole calls and thus measures call-to-call. The only
  estimator is the un-amortized min (the intercept fit), stuck
  at ±one ~10 ns quantum — on a ~1-11 ns quantity.

So the number we can measure precisely is not the number
subtraction wants, and the number subtraction wants cannot be
measured precisely. Consequences (0.21.0 cycle direction):

- Drop the framing term from the `adjusted` column — a
  quantized guess rendered at 3 decimals is false precision.
  Keep the loop/iter term: the amortized slope is measured to
  ±0.001 ns and dominates the per-call apparatus cost anyway.
- Size `inner` from the *call-to-call* constant: stable,
  conservative (over-sizing is harmless), and it removes the
  original harm — a low quantized framing draw under-sizing
  the experiment. The unsubtracted in-interval residue is then
  bounded by ~q/inner, roughly 1-2% of step cost, and can be
  stated as a bound instead of pretended away.
- The two-point window shape (M whole samples per window at
  N_LOW / N_HIGH) is the right call-to-call estimator: it
  keeps the real sample's pipelining context. We think this is
  why it reads lower than bare back-to-back pairs on r5-7600x
  (23.07 vs 32.36 ns — the loop gives the reads work to
  overlap with).

## Closed-loop mean identity

Why producer and consumer full means (and near enough their
min-p99 trimmed means) agree to ~0.1 ns within a run while
moving ~1.4% between runs (observed on r5-7600x tp-pc,
2026-07-13).

Each thread's probe intervals run back-to-back, so they tile
the run's wall-clock span. Both threads span the same wall
time and record the same count (every handoff appears once in

How to decide whether implementation A is really faster than B

systematic drift (mode mix, frequency regime, calibration).

harmless (bigger `inner`); under-estimating distorts.

### Fix: amortized framing measurement

Measure the timer-pair cost inside one window: one timer
read at the start, a loop of M back-to-back timer pairs, one
read at the end, divide by M. The ±1-quantum error on the
window amortizes to q/M per pair (~0.001 ns at M = 10,000) —
the same trick that already makes loop/iter steady.

Caveat: this measures the *throughput* cost of paired reads,
which can differ from a timer pair pipelined around real
work. We think it is still a far better subtraction constant
than "somewhere in a 10 ns interval", but it carries a
different (small) bias, not ground truth.

### Frequency dependence: what is constant, what is not

- The TSC rate and its ~10 ns quantum are invariant —
  constant across turbo, throttle, and idle states.
- The framing *cost* is core-clocked work (~tens of cycles
  of `rdtsc` + arithmetic), so its wall-clock value scales
  with core frequency: the same cycles take ~2× longer at a
  2.2 GHz throttle vs 4.6 GHz boost. Same for loop/iter.
- In practice calibration (post-warmup) and benches (hot
  loops) both run boosted, so the constants usually match.
  When frequency does shift, step cost shifts with framing
  cost, so contamination stays roughly proportional rather
  than blowing up; the subtraction just stops being exact.

So a cached calibration is a *machine + frequency-regime*
constant, not a universal one.

### Design: cached calibration in the config file

Store the calibration constants in the existing config file
(`src/config.rs`) rather than measuring fresh each run. The
primary benefit is run-to-run *comparability*, not startup
time: with a pinned adjustment constant, deltas between runs
reflect the bench, not the calibration lottery (~±0.23 ns on
adjusted values at inner = 43 today).

- An explicit calibrate command writes/refreshes the entry;
  runs use it when present, calibrate live otherwise.
- The entry carries provenance: CPU model, iiac-perf
  version, calibration date, raw `min_low`/`min_high`.
- Each run does a quick live amortized framing check
  (milliseconds) against the cached value: within a few
  percent, use the cache silently; off by more (throttle,
  different governor, stale file), warn or fall back to
  live. Cache validity becomes measured, not trusted.
- The report header states which mode adjusted the run —
  cached (with date) vs live — so a report is never
  ambiguous about its constants.

Rejected alternative: scaling calibration length with bench
duration (`-d` percentage). The residual error is
quantization, not sampling depth — more time in one
continuous measurement does not re-roll the phase alignment —
and calibration measures a machine property, not a bench
property.

### Trimmed core stats (p10-p90)

From a `tp-pc -d {5,10,20,50,60,100}` series on r5-7600x
(2026-07-13, v0.20.1-3), asking whether the report should add a
`mean/stdev p10-p90` or `p40-p60` row. The distribution is
strongly multi-modal: ~1% of handoffs at ~200 ns, ~9% smeared
over 0.25-3.6 us, a heavy plateau at 3.7-5.5 us, and a 1% tail
to ~400 us.

- The full `mean` wobbles ~±1.4% across the series
  (4,789-4,925 ns) and `mean min-p99` wobbles the same. We
  think the wobble is the *mode mix* (the p1-p10 share)
  shifting run to run, not noise in the plateau.
- The plateau center (p50-p60 band mean) is stable to ~±0.2%
  (5,378-5,402 ns) — a core-trimmed statistic is the
  run-to-run-comparable number, the same comparability goal
  as this cycle's cached calibration.
- Lean `p10-p90` (interdecile, a standard 10% trimmed mean)
  over `p40-p60`: the latter is essentially the median (the
  p50 boundary already shows it) and its stdev would mostly
  measure band quantization, not workload spread.
- An *additional* row, never a replacement: the fast modes are
  real behavior (e.g. consumer already waiting vs batched
  wakeups), so trimming must not hide them. Trim bounds are
  bench-shaped — consider config/flag (`--trim p10:p90`?)
  rather than hardcoding.
- Boundary sensitivity (4x20s series, r5-7600x, 0.21.0-3): a
  percentile-window mean is only as stable as its boundaries.
  p50-p60 (both edges inside the plateau) repeated to ±0.05%;
  p40-p50 wobbled ~1% because its lower edge rides the
  mode-mix smear (its `first` jumped 4,962 → 5,133 ns between
  runs). Percentiles count from the bottom, so any window edge
  in the smear inherits the mode-mix wobble — p10-p90 will
  beat the full mean but not reach plateau stability. We think
  the truly stable statistic is the dominant *mode* (the
  plateau's peak-density region), which doesn't depend on
  counting from the bottom.

so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
  invalidate.

Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —
with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's `# References`
(format in AGENTS.md
[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
SHA must be permanent.

## Preparation

The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
setup (a lightweight cycle omits it — see
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):

- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
  project-specific — see [versioning.md](versioning.md).
- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
  `## In Progress` and the todo item should have:
  - A **bold title line** — that will be the chores
    section header, minus the `## ` prefix.
  - A **succinct problem statement**; add if one is needed
  - A **plan ladder**.
- **Open the [chores section](#chores-sections)** —
  append a `##` header with the title it records — the
  cycle's anticipated close-out title.

## Work-N

The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, …)
implement the change. As many as needed:

- Each commit runs through the
  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
  visibility).
- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
  [Pushing](#pushing)).
- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
  scope grows enough (see
  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).

## Close-out

The cycle's last commit (bare `X.Y.Z`) does bookkeeping
only — the commit body describes that bookkeeping, not
what happens post-squash:

- **Move the picked-up item** from `## In Progress` to a
  one-line entry (with a chores `[N]` ref) in `## Done`.
- **Move the `## In Progress` block into the
  [chores section](#chores-sections)** (the title-only
  placeholder opened during Preparation):
  - Cut the problem statement + plan ladder out of
    `## In Progress` (drop the bold title line — the
    chores `##` header already carries that string).
  - Paste under the chores `##` header.
  - Sync the chores header to the **final** commit title
    if the cycle's scope shifted; update every anchor
    back-reference.
  - Add an `### As-built ladder` listing the cycle's
    commits; optional `### Outcome` notes.
  - Replace `## In Progress` with
    `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).

Titles carry **no trailing `(<version>)` suffix**. The
version-of-record — where it lives and its bump cadence, see
[versioning.md](versioning.md) — is useful for confirming
you're running the version you're testing, not a per-commit
title marker. We think per-commit version-in-title is
unstable on large projects: many changes are in flight
simultaneously, and a
version is only stable once merged into the main repo — so
titles don't carry one.

### Title

- ≤50 chars total.
- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
  `docs`, `chore`.
- Favor terse phrasings.
- **Distinct per step** — each of a cycle's commits gets its
  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them; the
  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
  AGENTS.md
  [Conventional-commit shape](../AGENTS.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).

[Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets),

Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time —
see [Pushing](#pushing).

## Numbering

Each commit's phase is encoded in the version suffix — `-0`
Preparation, `-1`/`-2`/… Work, bare `X.Y.Z` Close-out,
recursively for sub-cycles. The full scheme — disambiguation,
nesting, optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
format, and the per-phase bump — lives in
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering), which is the
single source of truth for this repo's versioning.

## Per-commit flow

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
through:

1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
   `notes/todo.md > ## In Progress`.
2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
   for the loop-and-squash technique).
3. **Flip this commit `(current)` → `(done)`** in `## In
   Progress` — before the cargo cycle and the commit.
4. **Validate the artifact** — a medium-specific step, skip-able
   for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. For the Rust
   example the cargo cycle is:
   1. `cargo fmt`
   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
   3. `cargo test`
   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
5. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description;
   tell the user "ready to commit." The user reviews the
   changes and we iterate until complete.
6. **Write the commit description** — see
   [Commit description](#commit-description).
7. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
8. **Commit.** `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R .` for
   the app repo, `-R .claude` for the bot repo (`-R` last
   keeps the verb visible):

   ```
   jj commit -m \
   "<type>: <short description>" \
   -m "<intro paragraph>

   - file1: gist
   - file2: gist

   ochid: /.claude/<chid>" \
   -R .
   ```

**Two overrides apply:**

- **Deviation or question** — any time the work deviates
  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
  surface it; don't push through.
- **ESC-ESC** — the user can interrupt at any point to pull
  a review or question forward.

195	### Design: cached calibration in the config file
196	
197	Store the calibration constants in the existing config file
198	(`src/config.rs`) rather than measuring fresh each run. The
199	primary benefit is run-to-run *comparability*, not startup
200	time: with a pinned adjustment constant, deltas between runs
201	reflect the bench, not the calibration lottery (~±0.23 ns on
202	adjusted values at inner = 43 today).
203	
204	- An explicit calibrate command writes/refreshes the entry;
205	  runs use it when present, calibrate live otherwise.
206	- The entry carries provenance: CPU model, iiac-perf
207	  version, calibration date, raw `min_low`/`min_high`.
208	- Each run does a quick live amortized framing check
209	  (milliseconds) against the cached value: within a few
210	  percent, use the cache silently; off by more (throttle,
211	  different governor, stale file), warn or fall back to
212	  live. Cache validity becomes measured, not trusted.
213	- The report header states which mode adjusted the run —
214	  cached (with date) vs live — so a report is never
215	  ambiguous about its constants.
216	
217	Rejected alternative: scaling calibration length with bench
218	duration (`-d` percentage). The residual error is
219	quantization, not sampling depth — more time in one
220	continuous measurement does not re-roll the phase alignment —
221	and calibration measures a machine property, not a bench
222	property.
223

message.content:
Calibration is actually quite quick I wonder if this is necessary?
One reason it might be is that it reduces inconsistent adjustments.
On the other hand if the hardware is altered let's say memory was
was upgraded or maybe even a CPU but using the same drives or the
test is on a removable media and the computer could change at any
invocation. Not right or wrong answer but I'm leaning towards always
running it. Thoughts?

content.text:
Good challenge — and I think the data from this very cycle supports your lean. Let me lay out the assessment.

## The case for the cache has been undermined by this cycle's own work

The design section is explicit that the cache was never about startup time (~150-200 ms, negligible against a 5 s default run). It was about killing the "calibration lottery" — the un-amortized ±10 ns quantum draw that made the adjustment constant wobble ~±0.23 ns run to run, so deltas between runs partly reflected calibration luck.

But that rationale was written *before* the mid-cycle dither revision. The dithered calibration that landed in -2/-3 already killed the lottery: `frame_sample` repeats to ±0.06 ns within a frequency regime and the slope is stable to 5 significant figures. At `inner ≈ 43` that's an adjustment wobble of roughly ±0.002 ns per call — three orders of magnitude below the run-to-run effects that actually dominate comparisons (the ~±1.4% mode-mix wobble the LSC methodology and the trimmed-stats work exist for). The cache would be solving a problem dithering already solved.

Meanwhile the cache's costs are real and yours is the sharpest version of them:

- A cached calibration is a *machine + frequency-regime* constant (design.md's own words). Removable media, a CPU swap, or even a throttled-vs-boosted day silently breaks the "same machine, same regime" assumption. Live calibration tracks the current regime by construction; a cache needs the -6 validity check as a patch for a hole it created itself.
- Provenance, staleness warnings, fallback logic, and a second config file are permanent complexity purchased for a benefit that is now ~±0.002 ns.

We think always-live is the better trade now: simpler, self-correcting under hardware/regime change, and the comparability argument no longer has teeth.

## What might still be worth keeping from -5

The standalone `calibrate` command has diagnostic value independent of any cache: run just the calibration and print the constants + raw fit points without running a bench. You've been doing exactly that kind of regime fingerprinting on both machines this cycle (today it requires `-v` plus a throwaway bench run). That half of -5 is cheap and useful; the config-cache half is the part that lost its justification.

Where things stand on disk: I'd already marked -5 `(current)` in todo.md, bumped Cargo.toml to 0.21.0-5, amended design.md for the calibration.toml decision, and refactored `config.rs` to expose `xdg_dir()`. Depending on your call I'll repurpose or revert those (the design.md section would get re-amended to record *this* decision and the why — a dropped plan is worth a written trace).

The plain version: we planned to measure the machine once and reuse the number, because the measurement used to be unreliable. We since made the measurement reliable, so reusing an old number no longer buys anything — and an old number can quietly go wrong if the machine changes. Measuring fresh every run is cheap, always current, and simpler.

content.content:
We should start simple, like comparing normal and async function calls and
later expand to other techniques.

## Usage

```
iiac-perf [BENCH...] [-d SECONDS] [-o OUTER] [-i INNER]
```

`BENCH` is one or more registered bench names, or `all` for every
registered bench. A name that matches no bench exactly runs every
bench it is a prefix of — `ice` runs all iceoryx2 benches, `mpsc`
runs `mpsc-1t` and `mpsc-2t`. **With no arguments, `iiac-perf` prints the
available list and exits — that's the source of truth for which
benches the current build registers.**

Flags (also visible via `-h` / `--help`):
- `-d`, `--duration SECONDS` — target wall-clock seconds per bench
  (default `5.0`); the outer loop runs until this time is reached
  (inner auto-sizes). See chores `0.3.1-dev1` for the empirical
  study behind the default — longer (`-d 30`+) gives
  publication-grade stability. Mutually exclusive with `-D`.
- `-D`, `--total-duration SECONDS` — target total wall-clock seconds
  across all requested benches; budget is split equally per bench
  (e.g. `-D 30` with 6 benches → 5 s each). Mutually exclusive with
  `-d`.
- `-o`, `--outer N` — override outer loop count (forces count-based
  mode instead of time-based; inner still adapts).
- `-i`, `--inner N` — override inner loop count per histogram sample.
  `inner=1` measures single-call latency (each sample = one step).
  Higher inner measures back-to-back / burst rate (each sample = N
  steps averaged, hides per-call jitter and parking costs).

  comma-separated list with optional ranges: `0,1`, `0-5`, `0,3-5,7`.

  thread `i` gets `pool[i % pool.len()]`. Examples:

  `--pin smt` with `smt = "0,12"` configured is exactly `--pin 0,12`.

  raw specs keep working.

  CPUs), logical IDs `N` and `N+12` are SMT siblings of the same
  physical core. `--pin 0,12` pairs siblings (max resource contention);
  `--pin 0,1` uses independent physical cores in the same CCX (best

content.content:
### Calibration banner

Every run calibrates apparatus overhead at startup and prints
three constants at 3 decimals (the dithered measurement resolves
well below a nanosecond):

- `frame/call` — the full call-to-call cost of taking one
  sample, both clock-read latencies included. It sizes the
  inner loop (`inner ≈ 10 × frame/call ÷ step cost`) and is
  never subtracted — most of it falls outside the recorded
  interval. See
  [in-interval vs call-to-call](notes/design.md#timer-overhead-in-interval-vs-call-to-call).
- `frame/sample` — the in-interval slice: what the timer pair
  actually adds *inside* a recorded sample. Measured by a
  dithered two-point fit — random sub-quantum delays before
  each calibration sample turn the ~10 ns clock quantization
  into zero-mean noise that averages away
  ([dithering](notes/design.md#dithering-random-phase-injection)).
  Subtracted from reported values, amortized by `inner`.
  Repeats to ~±0.1 ns within a CPU frequency regime
  ([validation](notes/design.md#dither-validation-results-0210-2-r5-7600x)).
- `loop/iter` — per-iteration loop overhead (branch +
  `black_box`), the fit's slope; subtracted per call. Repeats
  to 5 significant figures within a regime, so it doubles as
  a frequency-regime fingerprint.

The same dither runs between bench samples (the seam), so a
run's aggregate means don't inherit a coherent phase bias. All
three constants are machine- and frequency-regime-specific —
see
[Frequency dependence](notes/design.md#frequency-dependence-what-is-constant-what-is-not).
To decide whether a difference between two implementations is
real (and how many runs that takes), see
[Comparing implementations: LSC](notes/design.md#comparing-implementations-least-significant-change).

message.content: So "calibrate" is now reserved and can't be the name of a bench?

content.text:
Yes — exactly like `all` already is. Two words in the positional slot are now interpreted before bench resolution: `all` expands to every bench, and `calibrate` (exact match only) invokes the command. A bench registered under the literal name `calibrate` could never be run, because the command check happens first.

The blast radius is narrow, though:

- Only the exact string is reserved. Prefix invocations still work normally — typing `calib` goes through bench resolution, so a hypothetical `calibrate-2t` bench would still be runnable by full name or by any prefix except the exact string `calibrate`.
- No current bench is anywhere near the name (they're `ice-*`, `mpsc-*`, `zcr-*`, `tp-*`, etc.), and bench names are registered in-repo, so a future collision would be a deliberate choice, not an accident.

This was the trade for keeping the flat CLI: the alternatives were a clap subcommand restructure (`iiac-perf run <benches>` / `iiac-perf calibrate` — breaks every existing invocation) or a `--calibrate` flag (works, but reads oddly next to the bench-selection model). Reserved word matched the existing `all` precedent.

If you want the reservation enforced rather than just conventional, I can add a small test asserting no registered bench name equals a reserved word (`all`, `calibrate`), so a future registration that collides fails CI instead of being silently shadowed. Want that?

message.content: Why all the white space in the "after_help =" statement in the additional line?

content.text:
Those runs of whitespace are the *next* output line's indentation, awkwardly parked at the end of the previous source line. Two mechanics collide:

- In a Rust string literal, a `\` at the end of a line eats the newline **and all leading whitespace of the next source line**. That's what lets the continuation lines sit at normal source indentation without that indentation leaking into the string.
- Consequently, any spaces the *output* needs at the start of a line have to be written somewhere the `\` won't eat them — i.e. after the `\n`, before the trailing `\`.

So on the `all` line, `\n  \` means "newline, then 2 spaces indenting the next output line (`calibrate`)". On the `calibrate` line, `\n             \` is 13 spaces — that's 2 (left margin) + 9 (`calibrate`) + 2 (gap), aligning the wrapped description text under "run calibration…" in clap's two-column style:

```
  calibrate  run calibration only and print the constants plus the raw
             fit inputs (dithered points, alternative fits, ticks/ns).
```

It works, but the formatting intent is invisible — trailing spaces are unreadable and fragile under editing. A cleaner equivalent is `concat!`, where each output line is one source line with its leading spaces visible at the front where they logically belong:

```rust
after_help = concat!(
    "Commands:\n",
    "  all        run every registered bench\n",
    "  calibrate  run calibration only and print the constants plus the raw\n",
    "             fit inputs (dithered points, alternative fits, ticks/ns).\n",
    "             Must stand alone; --pin, --no-pin-cal, and -v apply as usual.",
),
```

The plain version: the spaces are there to indent the help text's next line; the backslash trick forces them to hide at the end of the line before, which is ugly. Want me to switch it to the `concat!` form so the layout is visible?

message.content: Since we're changing command line one other change, support command line completion, I believe that is "easy" although, IIRC, there is two techniques. Thoughts?

content.text:
Yes — completion is well-trodden with clap, and your memory is right: there are two techniques (arguably two-and-a-half). Thoughts on each:

**1. Static script generation (`clap_complete`, stable).** The CLI definition is rendered once into a shell-specific completion script (bash/zsh/fish/elvish/powershell). Two sub-variants — this may be the pair you remember:
- **Runtime flag**: a `--completions <shell>` flag (or another reserved word) that prints the script to stdout; you install it yourself once: `iiac-perf --completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/iiac-perf`. This is the standard modern approach for `cargo install`-distributed tools.
- **build.rs generation**: scripts are written into `OUT_DIR` at build time. Mainly useful for distro packagers who install the files as part of a package; for a `cargo install` workflow the files end up buried in `target/` where nobody finds them.

**2. Dynamic completion (`clap_complete` `CompleteEnv`, unstable API).** The binary completes *itself*: a one-line shim in your shell rc (`source <(COMPLETE=bash iiac-perf)`) calls back into the binary on every Tab. Its killer feature for us: it can complete **bench names** at runtime, always in sync with what the build registers. The static scripts can't do that well — our positional takes free-form names with prefix matching, and declaring `possible_values` to teach the script would make clap *validate* against the list, breaking prefix invocations like `ice`.

My recommendation: **static generation via a runtime flag** — stable API, one small dependency (`clap_complete`, same project as clap), ~15 lines, completes all flags plus whatever we choose to hint. Skip build.rs (wrong distribution model for this project) and skip dynamic for now (unstable API; worth revisiting once it stabilizes, since bench-name completion is genuinely attractive).

One process point: this doesn't belong in the -5 commit — `feat: calibrate diagnostic command` wouldn't honestly cover it, and the cycle protocol wants each step scoped to its title. I'd append a `0.21.0-6 feat: shell completion generation` step to the ladder and land -5 as already reviewed.

The plain version: we can either ship a pre-made autocomplete file you install once, or have the program answer the shell's autocomplete questions live. The pre-made file is the mature, simple option; the live one is fancier (it could suggest bench names) but relies on a not-yet-stable feature. I suggest the pre-made file, done as its own next commit.

# carapace-spec-clap

[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/carapace_spec_clap.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/carapace_spec_clap)

[Spec](https://github.com/carapace-sh/carapace-spec) generation for [clap-rs/clap](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap)

[![asciicast](https://asciinema.org/a/548145.svg)](https://asciinema.org/a/548145)

```rust
use carapace_spec_clap::Spec;
use clap::{Arg, ArgAction, Command, ValueHint};
use clap_complete::generate;
use std::io;

fn main() {
    let mut cmd = Command::new("example")
        .aliases(["alias1", "alias2"])
        .about("example command")
        .arg(
            Arg::new("help")
                .long("help")
                .short('h')
                .help("show help")
                .action(ArgAction::SetTrue),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("optional")
                .long("optional")
                .help("optional argument")
                .require_equals(true)
                .value_hint(ValueHint::Username),
        )
        .arg(
            Arg::new("value")
                .short('v')
                .help("takes argument")
                .value_parser(["one", "two", "three"]),
        )
        .subcommand(
            Command::new("subcommand")
                .about("example subcommand")
                .arg(
                    Arg::new("command")
                        .long("command")
                        .short('c')
                        .help("execute command")
                        .value_hint(ValueHint::CommandName),
                )
                .arg(
                    Arg::new("pos1")
                        .value_parser(["four", "five", "six"])
                        .value_hint(ValueHint::DirPath),
                )
                .arg(
                    Arg::new("posAny")
                        .num_args(1..)
                        .value_hint(ValueHint::Hostname),
                ),
        );

    generate(Spec, &mut cmd, "example", &mut io::stdout());
}
```

```yaml
aliases:
- alias1
- alias2
description: example command
flags:
  -h, --help: show help
  --optional?: optional argument
  -v=: takes argument

    - $carapace.os.Users
    v:
    - one
    - two
    - three
commands:
- name: subcommand
  description: example subcommand
  flags:
    -c, --command=: execute command
  completion:
    flag:
      command:
      - $executables
      - $files
    positional:
    - - $directories
      - four
      - five

```

content.text:
That's a good find, and it slots in more cleanly than I expected: `carapace_spec_clap::Spec` implements clap_complete's `Generator` trait — the exact same interface the static bash/zsh/fish generators use (`generate(Spec, &mut cmd, name, &mut stdout)`). So it isn't a third architecture; it's one more output format for technique 1.

That collapses the decision nicely:

- One `--completions <shell>` flag, where `<shell>` is `bash | zsh | fish | elvish | powershell | carapace`. The first five print classic static scripts (no external tooling needed); `carapace` prints the YAML spec for [carapace-bin](https://github.com/carapace-sh/carapace-bin), which then serves all of its shells from that one file. Users pick their poison; we maintain one code path.
- Cost: two dependencies (`clap_complete`, `carapace_spec_clap`), both stable APIs, and ~20 lines in main.
- The carapace route also leaves a door open for the thing static scripts can't do: carapace specs support exec-macros (`$(command …)`) for dynamic candidates, so a future step could teach the spec to complete bench names by invoking `iiac-perf` — without touching the unstable clap dynamic-completion API. The auto-generated spec won't have that yet, but the format allows it.

So my updated recommendation: the combined flag with all six generators, landed as a new ladder step `0.21.0-6 feat: shell completion generation` — and -5 (`calibrate` command) commits as already reviewed, since completions don't belong under its title.

Does that work for you — carapace + static generators behind one `--completions` flag as -6, with -5 committing first as reviewed? If so, I'll proceed to writing -5's commit description for your review, then open -6.

content.content:
vc-x1 0.68.0

Dual-repo commit+push+finalize in one resumable command.

Collapses today's manual Commit-Push-Finalize Flow into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (fmt/clippy/test) → review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-app → commit-claude (skipped if clean) → bookmark-set
(app → <bookmark>, session → main) → push-app →
finalize-claude. Failures in commit-app / commit-claude /
bookmark-set roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-app.
After push-app succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the code repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The session repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the code repo (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version
          Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then continue. With
          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

      --restart
          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --from <STAGE>
          Explicit stage to jump to (advanced / debug use)

          Possible values:
          - preflight:       Run fmt / clippy / test / install / retest
          - review:          Present diff for the first approval gate
          - message:         Compose / edit the commit message; present for
            second gate
          - commit-app:      Commit the app repo
          - commit-claude:   Commit the `.claude` session repo (skipped if
            empty)
          - bookmark-set:    Advance each repo's bookmark to its `@-`: app →
            `<bookmark>`, session → `main`
          - push-app:        `jj git push --bookmark <b> -R .`
          - finalize-claude: `vc-x1 finalize --repo .claude --squash --push main
            ...`

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --status
          Print where the saved state thinks we are and exit

      --recheck
          Re-run `preflight` even on resume (default: skip if last run
          succeeded)

      --no-finalize
          Stop before `finalize-claude` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

CPUs), logical IDs `N` and `N+12` are SMT siblings of the same
  physical core. `--pin 0,12` pairs siblings (max resource contention);
  `--pin 0,1` uses independent physical cores in the same CCX (best
  latency for channel benches — shared L3, no SMT contention). Check
  your topology with
  `cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/topology/thread_siblings_list`.

  Typical measured effect on `mpsc-2t` at `-d 10` (3900X, idle desktop):
  unpinned mean ≈ 7,044 ns / stdev ≈ 6,545 ns / p99.99 ≈ 74 µs;
  `--pin 0,1` → mean ≈ 5,636 ns / stdev ≈ 1,321 ns / p99.99 ≈ 17 µs.
  Tail tightens ~4×, stdev ~5×, mean drops ~20 %.
- `--no-pin-cal` — skip pinning the main thread for calibration.
  By default, calibration runs with main pinned to `pin[0]` (if
  `--pin` is set) or core 0, so framing/loop numbers come from a
  stable environment regardless of `--pin`. Pass this flag to
  reproduce pre-0.6.0 behavior (main pinned iff `--pin` is given)
  for A/B comparison. No effect when `--pin` is set.
- `-v`, `--verbose` — print internals to stderr (affinity mask at
  startup, calibration parameters, the raw dithered points and
  window value, the three alternative fits, calibration wall
  time). Equivalent to `RUST_LOG=debug`. Default filter is
  `warn` — silent unless something is wrong. `RUST_LOG`, when
  set, wins over `-v` so per-module filtering still works.
- `--band-labels STYLE` — label style for the histogram rows:
  `zpn` (nines/zeros + decile names: `z3`, `p50`, `n4`), `frac`
  (literal boundary fractions with `_` grouping: `0.001`, `0.50`,
  `0.999_9`), or `both` (default) — zpn and fraction side by
  side; the juxtaposition teaches the zpn vocabulary, switch to
  `zpn` once fluent. The report header records the active style
  as `labels=<style>` so saved outputs are self-describing.
- `--decimals N` — decimal digits on the report's time columns
  (0–3). Default 1 shows the sub-ns precision that picosecond
  recording captures (values are recorded internally in ps and
  displayed in ns); `0` restores integer ns; `3` is the
  recording floor — more digits would be artifacts.
- `--blocks N` — N (2–1000) is the **number of measurement
  blocks** the run's budget is divided into: `--blocks 10`
  with `-d 10` measures 10 blocks of ~1 s each (total measured
  time still 10 s; with `-o` the sample count is divided
  instead). Between blocks the harness sleeps a random 1–10 ms
  (fixed internal range — it re-rolls scheduler/frequency
  state) and warms up unrecorded (~2 ms); neither is counted
  in the budget. The report gains three lines — `mean blocks`
  (mean of the N block means), `CI95` (95% **c**onfidence
  **i**nterval half-width on it), and `LSC` (**l**east
  **s**ignificant **c**hange vs an equal-N run) — and the
  header records `blocks=N`. N is also the statistical
  replication count: more blocks → tighter CI but shorter
  blocks. Interpretation: an honest *within-invocation* error
  bar; treat it as a lower bound on cross-invocation
  confidence and pin the bench (`--pin`) — unpinned,
  per-process thread placement dominates and blocks can't see
  it. Bench-driven benches only; probe benches ignore it. See
  [validation](notes/design.md#block-validation-results-0210-4-r5-7600x)
  and the
  [design](notes/design.md#within-invocation-replication-sleep-separated-blocks).
- `--no-inhibit` — do not inhibit system sleep for the run. By
  default the process re-execs itself under
  `systemd-inhibit --what=sleep` so an idle-suspend can't poison a
  long measurement (a mid-sample suspend inflates that sample by
  the whole sleep gap; see the `WARNING` lines below). Where
  `systemd-inhibit` is unavailable — absent, or the lock is
  denied (e.g. a headless ssh session with no polkit
  interactive auth) — the run continues uninhibited and the
  banner's `sleep inhibit` line says so. Pass this flag to
  keep the process image untouched (strace/gdb/perf wrappers), to

  --completions=: 'Print a shell-completion artifact to stdout and exit (no bench runs): a static script for bash/zsh/fish/elvish/ powershell, or a spec for the carapace-bin multi-shell engine.   -d, --duration=: Target wall-clock seconds per bench (default 5.0, or the config `duration`). Auto-sizes outer and inner loop counts. Mutually exclusive with -D
  -h, --help: Print help (see more with '--help')
  -i, --inner=: Override inner loop count (skips auto-sizing). inner=1 measures single-call latency (each sample = one step); higher inner measures back-to-back/burst rate (each sample = N steps averaged)
  --no-inhibit: Do not inhibit system sleep for the run. By default the process re-execs itself under `systemd-inhibit --what=sleep` so an idle-suspend can't poison a long measurement. Pass this to keep the process image untouched (strace/gdb/perf wrappers), to let the machine sleep on purpose, or to test the suspend-detection WARNING path (a sleep inhibitor also blocks manual `systemctl suspend`)
  --no-pin-cal: Skip pinning the main thread for calibration. Always takes effect, including when `--pin` is set — bench threads still pin per `--pin`, but main stays on whatever affinity mask the process launched with. By default (without this flag), calibration runs with main pinned to `pin[0]` if set, else core 0, so framing/loop come from a stable environment. Pass this flag to decouple the calibration environment from the bench pinning pool (or to reproduce pre-0.6.0 behavior when `--pin` is absent)
  -o, --outer=: Override outer loop count (skips auto-sizing; inner still adapts)
  --pin=: 'Pin bench threads to logical CPUs (comma-separated, ranges OK). The list is a core *pool*: thread `i` of a bench is pinned to `pool[i % pool.len()]`, so shorter pools oversubscribe by wrap. Examples: `--pin 0,1` (2 threads → 2 CPUs), `--pin 0-5` (6-thread pool), `--pin 0,0` (two threads on the same CPU). On 3900X, logical CPUs N and N+12 are SMT siblings of the same physical core — `--pin 0,12` pairs siblings (max contention), `--pin 0,1` gives independent cores. A value naming a `[profiles]` entry in the config file expands to that profile''s core spec (e.g. `--pin smt`). Omit to leave threads unpinned'
  -t, --ticks: Show tprobe results in raw TSC ticks instead of converting to nanoseconds. Only affects `TProbe` output; `Probe` results are always in nanoseconds

  --no-inhibit: Do not inhibit system sleep for the run. By default the process re-execs itself under `systemd-inhibit --what=sleep` so an idle-suspend can't poison a long measurement. Pass this to keep the process image untouched (strace/gdb/perf wrappers), to let the machine sleep on purpose, or to test the suspend-detection WARNING path (a sleep inhibitor also blocks manual `systemctl suspend`)
  --no-pin-cal: Skip pinning the main thread for calibration. Always takes effect, including when `--pin` is set — bench threads still pin per `--pin`, but main stays on whatever affinity mask the process launched with. By default (without this flag), calibration runs with main pinned to `pin[0]` if set, else core 0, so framing/loop come from a stable environment. Pass this flag to decouple the calibration environment from the bench pinning pool (or to reproduce pre-0.6.0 behavior when `--pin` is absent)
  -o, --outer=: Override outer loop count (skips auto-sizing; inner still adapts)
  --pin=: 'Pin bench threads to logical CPUs (comma-separated, ranges OK). The list is a core *pool*: thread `i` of a bench is pinned to `pool[i % pool.len()]`, so shorter pools oversubscribe by wrap. Examples: `--pin 0,1` (2 threads → 2 CPUs), `--pin 0-5` (6-thread pool), `--pin 0,0` (two threads on the same CPU). On 3900X, logical CPUs N and N+12 are SMT siblings of the same physical core — `--pin 0,12` pairs siblings (max contention), `--pin 0,1` gives independent cores. A value naming a `[profiles]` entry in the config file expands to that profile''s core spec (e.g. `--pin smt`). Omit to leave threads unpinned'
  -t, --ticks: Show tprobe results in raw TSC ticks instead of converting to nanoseconds. Only affects `TProbe` output; `Probe` results are always in nanoseconds
  -D, --total-duration=: Target total wall-clock seconds across all requested benches; budget is split equally per bench. Mutually exclusive with -d
  -v, --verbose: 'Enable verbose internals on stderr: affinity mask, cal parameters and raw fit inputs, calibration wall time. Equivalent to `RUST_LOG=debug`. Default is `warn` (silent unless something''s wrong). `RUST_LOG` overrides this flag when set, so per-module filtering still works'
  -V, --version: Print version

If you want a live test, `source <(iiac-perf --completions bash)` in your shell and Tab on `iiac-perf --`.

One honest limitation to be aware of before you sign off: completion covers flags and their values, but not bench names or the `all`/`calibrate` words — those are free-form positionals to clap. The carapace exec-macro route could add that later; I noted it in the README and it could become a Todo entry if you care.

message.content: So carapace spec doesn't provide for communication with the app in the dynamic sense, it expects each app to build a .yaml which is a static database of "parameter/commands" for the app?

content.text:
Close, but the spec format is a bit more capable than a static database. Three layers to distinguish:

- **The spec file itself is static** — one YAML per app, generated once, describing flags/commands/descriptions. What `carapace_spec_clap` auto-generates for us today is exactly that: a snapshot of what clap knows at generation time. That's why bench names aren't in it.
- **But the spec's candidate lists can contain macros, evaluated at Tab-time.** You can see two flavors in the README example we fetched earlier: built-ins like `$carapace.os.Users`, `$files`, `$executables` (carapace-bin resolves these itself when you press Tab), and the exec macro `$(some command)`, which runs an arbitrary command *at completion time* and uses its stdout lines as candidates. So a spec can absolutely communicate with the app dynamically — it's just that the *hook* is declared statically in the YAML. For us that would look like the positional's completion being something like `$(iiac-perf --list-benches)`, with the app growing a machine-readable list flag. Every Tab press would then ask the live binary, so candidates always match the installed build.
- **Full dynamic completion** (the clap `CompleteEnv` route we set aside) goes further: there's no spec at all — the shell asks the binary itself to complete every word. That's the unstable-API option.

So: what we generate today is static; the format supports declared dynamic callbacks; the auto-generator just doesn't emit any (it can't know a `--list-benches` exists). Getting dynamic bench names via carapace would mean adding a list flag to the app and either post-processing the generated spec or emitting that one macro line ourselves.

The plain version: the YAML is a fixed menu, but a menu entry is allowed to say "run this program and offer whatever it prints." We don't use that trick yet — our generated file only lists what was known when it was written. If we later want Tab to offer bench names, we'd add that one "ask the app" line.

message.content: In this app we do know all the commands at compile time so we should be able to add them to the yaml file, correct?

content.text:
Correct — the bench registry is compiled in (`src/benches/mod.rs`), so `benches::names()` is available to the generation code path at runtime of `--completions`, and we can inject the full list into the spec. The wrinkle is *where* it can go:

- **Carapace spec: yes, cleanly.** Generate the YAML into a buffer, then insert a `positionalany:` candidate list under the existing `completion:` key — `all` and `calibrate` (with `\t`-separated descriptions, which carapace renders next to the candidate) plus every bench name. Carapace only *offers* candidates, it never rejects input, so prefix invocations like `ice` keep working while Tab offers the full names.
- **Static bash/zsh/fish scripts: not really.** clap's static generators only emit positional candidates from declared `possible_values`, and declaring those makes clap *validate* the positional — `iiac-perf ice` would then be rejected as "not one of…", breaking prefix matching. Patching six shell scripts textually instead is per-shell surgery I'd avoid. So bench-name completion becomes a carapace-exclusive nicety, which is fair — that's the engine built for it.

It's a small addition (~20 lines plus a unit test on the patched YAML) and sits squarely under the `feat: shell completion generation` title, so it can fold into -6 before we commit. Note this is the *static-list* variant of what we discussed: the spec snapshots the names at generation time, so it needs regenerating when benches are added — the `$(iiac-perf --list)` exec-macro variant would stay live but needs a new listing flag; that can remain future work.

Want me to add the carapace `positionalany` injection to -6?

# Bridge

Bridging completions from another engine for shells not natively supported by it is possible with the corresponding [Macro](./macros.md).

> Even when the command supports your current shell it is still beneficial to bridge it as this enables [embedding](./embed.md) like `sudo [spec.name] <TAB>`.
>
> It also avoids the issue of shell startup delay when sourcing the completion in init scripts otherwise circumvented with [lazycomplete].
>
> However, bridging is limited to supported commands/frameworks and how well it actually works.


## Frameworks

### Argcomplete

[kislyuk/argcomplete] based commands can be bridged with the [`bridge.Argcomplete`] macro:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://carapace.sh/schemas/command.json
name: az
description: Azure Command-Line Interface
parsing: disabled
completion:
  positionalany: ["$carapace.bridge.Argcomplete([az])"]
```

### Carapace

[carapace-sh/carapace] based commands can be bridged with the [`bridge.Carapace`] macro:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://carapace.sh/schemas/command.json
name: freckles
description: simple dotfile manager
parsing: disabled
completion:
  positionalany: ["$carapace.bridge.Carapace([freckles])"]
```

### CarapaceBin

[Completers](../completers.md) and [Specs](../spec.md) registered in [carapace-sh/carapace-bin] can be bridged with the [`bridge.CarapaceBin`] macro:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://carapace.sh/schemas/command.json
name: github-cli
description: Work seamlessly with GitHub from the command line
parsing: disabled
completion:
  positionalany: ["$carapace.bridge.CarapaceBin([gh])"]
```

### Clap

[clap-rs/clap] based commands can be bridged with the [`bridge.Clap`] macro:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://carapace.sh/schemas/command.json
name: dyamic
description: clap dynamic example
parsing: disabled
completion:
  positionalany: ["$carapace.bridge.Clap([dynamic])"]
```

> needs [clap-rs/clap#3166](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/issues/3166)

### Click

[pallets/click] based commands can be bridged with the [`bridge.Click`] macro:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://carapace.sh/schemas/command.json
name: watson
description: Watson is a tool aimed at helping you monitoring your time
parsing: disabled
completion:
  positionalany: ["$carapace.bridge.Click([watson])"]
```

### Cobra

[spf13/cobra] based commands can be bridged with the [`bridge.Cobra`] macro:

```yaml
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://carapace.sh/schemas/command.json
name: kubectl
description: kubectl controls the Kubernetes cluster manager
parsing: disabled
completion:
  positionalany: ["$carapace.bridge.Cobra([kubectl])"]
```

### Complete
[posener/complete] based commands can be bridged with the [`bridge.Complete`] macro:


# Bridge

Bridging completions from another engine for shells not natively supported by it is possible with the corresponding [Macro](./macros.md).

> Even when the command supports your current shell it is still beneficial to bridge it as this enables [embedding](./embed.md) like `sudo [spec.name] <TAB>`.
>
> It also avoids the issue of shell startup delay when sourcing the completion in init scripts otherwise circumvented with [lazycomplete].
>
> However, bridging is limited to supported commands/frameworks and how well it actually works.

### Argcomplete

content.text:
Here's the full picture (carapace-bin itself isn't installed on this machine yet, by the way):

**Yes — the "full dynamic"路 route is supported by carapace today, but it doesn't eliminate the unstable clap API; it *contains* it.** The two pieces:

- **carapace side (shipping now):** a five-line user spec bridges the whole command dynamically — `parsing: disabled` plus `positionalany: ["$carapace.bridge.Clap([iiac-perf])"]`. Carapace then forwards every Tab press to the binary and relays its answers, for every shell carapace supports. No per-flag YAML, nothing to regenerate when the CLI changes.
- **app side (the catch):** `bridge.Clap` works by invoking the binary's *native dynamic completion protocol* — exactly the clap #3166 / `clap_complete` `unstable-dynamic` feature you remembered. Carapace doesn't introspect clap binaries by magic; the app must answer the completion protocol. So we'd enable that unstable feature and add the `CompleteEnv` hook (~5 lines early in `main`), plus optionally `ArgValueCandidates` on the positional — which, notably, supplies bench-name candidates *without* the validation problem that blocked the static route.

The risk calculus is better than raw unstable-dynamic, though. If the unstable protocol changes in a future clap release, the blast radius is one `cargo update` + a carapace-bridge update — the shells only ever talk to carapace, whose interface is stable, and the bridge spec never changes. Compare that with native `CompleteEnv` shims in your rc files, where a protocol change breaks each shell's integration directly. So carapace acts as the stable façade over the unstable core — "vulnerable to never being stabilized" becomes "pinned dependency risk," which is a much more ordinary kind of risk.

The plain version: carapace can already ask a program live "what should Tab offer here?" — but only if the program speaks the not-yet-final clap dialect for answering. Carapace stands in the middle, so if that dialect shifts, only the carapace↔program joint needs re-gluing, not your shell setup.

Practical proposal: land -6 as reviewed (static scripts + generated spec are useful regardless, and are the fallback for people without carapace), then add a `0.21.0-7 feat: clap dynamic completion bridge` step: `unstable-dynamic` feature, `CompleteEnv` hook, bench-name candidates, README section with the bridge spec — and you'd install carapace-bin to try it live. Want to go that way, or fold the dynamic piece into -6?

content.text:
Answers to both, from current sources:

**Shells carapace-bin supports today:** Bash, Zsh, Fish, PowerShell, Elvish, Nushell, Oil, Xonsh — plus Cmd, Ion, and Tcsh marked experimental. So it covers everything our static generators emit, plus the ones clap has no generator for (Nushell, Xonsh, Oil…).

**Is there a crate implementing the carapace side directly? No.** The crates.io search turns up exactly one carapace-ecosystem crate: `carapace_spec_clap` — the spec generator we're already using. (The crate literally named `carapace` is an unrelated online-judge tool.) The carapace *engine* — the thing that answers shells and evaluates specs — exists only as the Go library/binary. Its app-facing protocol (the `_carapace export` interface Go apps embed) isn't published as a spec for third-party implementations, so "implement carapace's protocol natively in Rust" would mean reverse-engineering a private interface that's free to change — worse footing than clap's unstable API, which is at least *intended* to stabilize.

That leaves two honest "direct" designs, and it turns out the bridge distinction mostly dissolves:

1. **Exec-macro spec — dynamic bench names, zero unstable APIs.** The app grows a tiny machine-readable listing flag (say `--list-benches`), and the generated carapace spec completes the positional with `$(iiac-perf --list-benches)`. Every Tab press asks the live binary, so names never go stale. Everything involved — the spec format, exec macros, our flag — is stable. Carapace covers all eleven shells. This *is* direct app communication; no bridge macro involved.
2. **clap dynamic (`CompleteEnv`, unstable) — full dynamic parsing.** The binary answers the whole completion dialog (flags too, mid-word, context-aware). Native shims cover bash/zsh/fish/elvish/powershell; `bridge.Clap` extends it to carapace's other shells. This is the "right" architecture long-term, but it's the unstable-API exposure you identified.

My recommendation: option 1 as the next step — it gets you the thing you actually wanted (live bench-name completion, carapace as the universal engine) with no unstable surface at all. Option 2 can layer on later once clap stabilizes dynamic completion, without undoing anything.

The plain version: nobody has rewritten carapace's brain in Rust — only a helper that writes its config files. But we don't need it: the config file can contain "ask the program for the list," which gives live names using only stable pieces. The fancier live-everything mode still requires clap's not-yet-final feature, bridge or no bridge.

content.text:
Almost exactly right — two refinements, one small and one that matters for the design:

**Refinement 1 — who installs what.** Even with -6 as is, a given user never needs *every* script — they install the one artifact for their shell: a static script if they're a plain bash/zsh/fish user, or the yaml if they run carapace. What the exec-macro option changes is that the carapace path becomes strictly better than the scripts (live bench names), so the yaml becomes the recommended install and the static scripts remain a no-carapace fallback (they're already written; keeping them costs nothing). Also note the yaml isn't understood by shells directly — the user installs carapace-bin once and adds its one-line hook to their shell rc; from then on carapace serves all eleven shells from that single yaml. So "one yaml + one engine" rather than "one yaml, period."

**Refinement 2 — who does the matching.** With the exec-macro design, our sub-command (really a flag, `--list-benches`) is invoked on Tab, but it does **not** receive what the user typed and doesn't do the completion logic. It just prints the full candidate list, one per line; *carapace* filters that list against the word under the cursor and renders the menu. So for `iiac-perf ice<tab>`: carapace runs `iiac-perf --list-benches`, gets all 17+ names, filters to the `ice*` ones, and shows `ice-ps-1t  ice-ps-2t  ice-rr-1t  ice-rr-2t`. The outcome is exactly what you described — we just don't have to implement prefix matching, cursor parsing, or any per-keystroke protocol; our side stays a dumb, stable "print the list" flag. (Carapace *can* pass the current word to an exec-macro via an environment variable if a command ever wants smarter server-side filtering, but we don't need it.)

And yes — no multi-script writing or installing. One generated yaml in `~/.config/carapace/specs/`, and every carapace-hooked shell gets flag completion *and* live bench names that stay correct as benches are added, because the list comes from the installed binary at Tab-time.

content.text:
Concrete steps on a fresh machine, both cases assuming `cargo install --path .` (or however the binary arrives) has happened:

**With -6 as is:**

- *Plain-shell user (no carapace), e.g. bash:*
  1. `iiac-perf --completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/iiac-perf` (dir exists once the distro's `bash-completion` package is installed; zsh/fish users write their shell's file instead).
  2. Open a new shell.
  3. Tab now completes flags and flag values (`--band-labels <tab>` → `zpn frac both`), but **not** bench names.
  4. After upgrading iiac-perf, regenerate the file — it's a snapshot.
- *Carapace user:*
  1. Install carapace-bin once (on Arch: `pacman -S carapace`; otherwise a GitHub release binary).
  2. Add its one-line hook to the shell rc once per shell, e.g. bash: `source <(carapace _carapace bash)`.
  3. `iiac-perf --completions carapace > ~/.config/carapace/specs/iiac-perf.yaml`.
  4. Same completion coverage as the static script (flags only), same regenerate-after-upgrade caveat — but steps 1–2 are per-machine/per-shell, not per-app, and cover all their shells at once.

**With -7:** the carapace user's steps are *identical* — install carapace-bin, hook the shell, write the one yaml. Nothing extra to do. What changes is what Tab delivers:

- `iiac-perf ice<tab>` now offers `ice-ps-1t ice-ps-2t ice-rr-1t ice-rr-2t`, because the spec's exec-macro asks the installed binary for the live list on every Tab.
- Bench names never go stale — add a bench, rebuild, and completion is current with no regeneration, because the names come from the binary, not the file.
- The *flag* portion of the yaml is still a snapshot, so the regenerate-after-upgrade advice remains for CLI-surface changes (new/renamed flags) — just not for benches.
- Plain-shell users without carapace are unchanged from -6: static scripts, flags only.

So -7 costs the user nothing beyond what the carapace path in -6 already asks; it only upgrades the payoff. The step counts are: plain shell = 1 command per app per upgrade; carapace = 2 one-time machine/shell setup steps + 1 command per app.

content.text:
Correct, with one asterisk: nothing extra to *install* — no carapace, no script files — but there is one line of shell config. The user puts this in their `.bashrc` (equivalents exist for zsh, fish, elvish, powershell):

```bash
source <(COMPLETE=bash iiac-perf)
```

That's the whole setup. On shell startup the binary emits a tiny shim; on every Tab the shim calls back into `iiac-perf` itself, which parses the partial command line and answers. And this design has a property the file-based routes can't match: since the shim is regenerated from the binary at every shell startup, upgrading iiac-perf automatically upgrades completion — there is no stale artifact anywhere, for flags *or* benches.

Coverage with the dynamic API:

- Flags and flag values, context-aware (it knows what you've already typed).
- Bench names on the positional — we attach a candidate provider (`ArgValueCandidates`) that returns `benches::names()` plus `all`/`calibrate`, with descriptions. No validation problem: candidates don't constrain what clap accepts, so prefix invocations like `iiac-perf ice` keep working.
- Shells: bash, zsh, fish, elvish, powershell natively. Nushell/xonsh/oil users would still reach it via carapace's `bridge.Clap` — which consumes this same protocol, so that comes free.

The instability risk lands on *us*, not users: the `unstable-dynamic` feature's Rust API can shift between clap_complete releases, so a `cargo update` might need code tweaks. The user-facing rc line is insulated — it just asks the binary for whatever the current shim is.

On "-6 is useless": fair verdict for your workflow, though I'd keep its code — the static generators are ~30 lines, already tested, and remain the only offline option (plus `--completions carapace` becomes the bridge-spec delivery vehicle). My suggestion: commit -6 as built, then `0.21.0-7 feat: dynamic completion` adds the `unstable-dynamic` feature, the `CompleteEnv` hook, and the bench-name candidate provider — after which the one rc line gives you everything, and we see whether `iiac-perf ice<tab>` really dances.

The plain version: yes — with the unstable-API route the program answers Tab itself, so there's nothing to install and nothing to keep fresh; you add a single line to your shell's startup file once. The gamble is only that the feature we build on is still marked "may change," which we absorb at compile time, not you at the keyboard.

content.text:
Agreed — that's unreadable. The root cause is on our side, not carapace's: clap derives two help strings from a doc comment — `help` (short, meant for `-h` and completion menus) and `long_help` (full, for `--help`). The split happens at the **first blank line** of the doc comment. Our arg doc comments have no blank lines, so short help *is* the entire paragraph, and every consumer — `-h`, the spec, the Tab menu — gets the wall of text (truncated at ~78 chars in the menu).

The clean fix is to restructure each arg's doc comment to the clap convention: a one-line summary, blank line, then the detail. Example for `--duration`:

```rust
/// Target wall-clock seconds per bench.
///
/// Default 5.0, or the config `duration`; auto-sizes outer and
/// inner loop counts. Mutually exclusive with -D.
```

Effects across the three surfaces:

- **Tab menu**: `--duration (Target wall-clock seconds per bench.)` — scannable.
- **`-h`**: becomes a compact summary listing (one line per flag) instead of today's full paragraphs.
- **`--help`**: unchanged — full detail, nothing lost.

The one real trade-off is that `-h` gets much terser. I'd call that an improvement (it matches how every other clap tool behaves, and `--help` keeps the depth), but it is a visible change to output you're used to. The alternative — post-processing the YAML to truncate descriptions while leaving doc comments alone — keeps `-h` verbose but adds fragile string surgery and only fixes one of the three surfaces; I don't recommend it.

If you're good with the doc-comment restructure, I'd fold it into -7 (it's the completion UX, and the commit isn't pushed yet) — it touches every `#[arg]` doc comment in `main.rs`, summary lines chosen so nothing informative is lost from `--help`. Proceed that way?

content.text:
Carapace handles that natively — the spec format is a *tree*, not a flat list. A spec can carry a `commands:` array where each entry is a full command node with its own `flags:`, its own `completion:` block, and even nested `commands:` of its own. You can see the shape in the carapace-spec-clap README example we fetched earlier — the generated spec for a clap app with a subcommand came out like:

```yaml
name: example
flags:
  -h, --help: show help          # root flags
commands:
- name: subcommand
  description: example subcommand
  flags:
    -c, --command=: execute command   # subcommand-only flags
  completion:
    positional:
    - [$directories, four, five, six]
```

At Tab-time carapace parses the words before the cursor, walks down the tree (`vc-x1 sync …` → the `sync` node), and completes from that node only — so `vc-x1 init -<Tab>` would offer `--account`/`--por`/`--use-template` while `vc-x1 sync -<Tab>` offers `--bookmark`/`--remote`/`--rebase`. Per-subcommand usage shapes are exactly what the tree encodes. And `carapace_spec_clap` builds that tree automatically from clap's own subcommand structure — an app like vc-x1 would get its whole `init`/`sync`/`push` hierarchy in one generated YAML with zero hand-editing. (vc-x1 today gets equivalent behavior a different way: its `COMPLETE=bash vc-x1` hook has the binary itself parse the partial line, and clap knows its own subcommand tree.)

The reason our spec has no `commands:` section is honest: we don't have clap subcommands. `all` and `calibrate` are reserved words inside a positional, so clap — and therefore the generated spec — sees one flat grammar where every flag is global. That matches reality (`iiac-perf calibrate --pin 3` is genuinely valid), with one small blemish: after `calibrate`, Tab still offers flags calibrate ignores (`--duration`, `--blocks`), because nothing in the grammar scopes them. If that ever bothers us, the fix is to promote the words to real clap subcommands — the generator would then nest them and carapace would scope flags per word automatically — but that's a breaking CLI restructure, which is why we went reserved-words in the first place.

The plain version: the yaml isn't one flat list — it can hold a branch per subcommand, each with its own flags, and carapace picks the branch matching what's typed so far. Tools with real subcommands get per-command menus for free; ours shows one shared menu because our commands really do share one flag set.

_carapace_completer() {
  export COMP_LINE
  export COMP_POINT
  export COMP_TYPE
  export COMP_WORDBREAKS

  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL=bash
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_ALIASES="$(compgen -a)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_BUILTINS="$(compgen -b)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_FUNCTIONS="$(compgen -A function)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_JOBS="$(jobs 2>/dev/null | while read -r line; do [[ $line =~ \[([0-9]+)\] ]] && echo "%${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"; done)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_VARIABLES="$(compgen -v)"

  local command="${COMP_WORDS[0]}" nospace data compline="${COMP_LINE:0:${COMP_POINT}}"

  data=$(echo "${compline}''" | xargs carapace "${command}" bash 2>/dev/null)
  if [ $? -eq 1 ]; then
    data=$(echo "${compline}'" | xargs carapace "${command}" bash 2>/dev/null)
    if [ $? -eq 1 ]; then
    	data=$(echo "${compline}\"" | xargs carapace "${command}" bash 2>/dev/null)
    fi
  fi

  IFS=$'\001' read -r -d '' nospace data <<<"${data}"
  mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(echo "${data}")
  unset COMPREPLY[-1]

  [ "${nospace}" = true ] && compopt -o nospace
  local IFS=$'\n'
  [[ "${COMPREPLY[*]}" == "" ]] && COMPREPLY=() # fix for mapfile creating a non-empty array from empty command output
}
