_carapace_completer() {
  export COMP_LINE
  export COMP_POINT
  export COMP_TYPE
  export COMP_WORDBREAKS

  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL=bash
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_ALIASES="$(compgen -a)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_BUILTINS="$(compgen -b)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_FUNCTIONS="$(compgen -A function)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_JOBS="$(jobs 2>/dev/null | while read -r line; do [[ $line =~ \[([0-9]+)\] ]] && echo "%${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"; done)"
  declare -x CARAPACE_SHELL_VARIABLES="$(compgen -v)"

  local command="${COMP_WORDS[0]}" nospace data compline="${COMP_LINE:0:${COMP_POINT}}"

  data=$(echo "${compline}''" | xargs carapace "${command}" bash 2>/dev/null)
  if [ $? -eq 1 ]; then
    data=$(echo "${compline}'" | xargs carapace "${command}" bash 2>/dev/null)
    if [ $? -eq 1 ]; then
    	data=$(echo "${compline}\"" | xargs carapace "${command}" bash 2>/dev/null)
    fi
  fi

  IFS=$'\001' read -r -d '' nospace data <<<"${data}"
  mapfile -t COMPREPLY < <(echo "${data}")
  unset COMPREPLY[-1]

  [ "${nospace}" = true ] && compopt -o nospace
  local IFS=$'\n'
  [[ "${COMPREPLY[*]}" == "" ]] && COMPREPLY=() # fix for mapfile creating a non-empty array from empty command output
}

content.text:
Reproduced — and that settles both questions:

**The alignment:** not achievable from our side in bash. Carapace's bash writer fuses each candidate into a single string — `--flag (description)` — before bash ever sees it, and readline just prints those strings; there is no separate "description column" to align (bash has no native description support at all — that's the gap carapace is papering over). The knob that *does* exist is the one I tested above: `CARAPACE_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` trims descriptions, so adding e.g.

```bash
export CARAPACE_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH=45
```

to your `.bashrc` tames the line lengths. True two-column alignment would need carapace's bash writer to pad the value part — a reasonable upstream feature request for carapace-sh/carapace, but not something our spec can express. Worth knowing: the shells with native description menus — zsh, fish, nushell — render exactly the aligned two-column view you're asking for, out of the same spec, with no configuration (zsh even merges the `-d`/`--duration` pairs side-by-side by default).

**The "extra space":** intentional, and kind of clever. Notice all 24 candidates share the prefix `--`/`-`; left alone, readline would *insert* that common prefix instead of showing the menu. Carapace defeats that by prepending a space to the first candidate ('` --band-labels …`'), making the common prefix empty so readline is forced to display the list. It's display-only — never inserted into your command line.

So my suggestion: set `CARAPACE_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` to taste in your `.bashrc` (that's user config, like the hook line), and I can add a one-line tip about it to the README's Shell completion section since every bash user of the spec will hit the same reaction. Beyond that, nothing in our repo can move this further — it's carapace's renderer.

content.text:
Confirmed on both fronts:

- vc-x1 uses exactly that: `clap_complete = { features = ["unstable-dynamic"] }` and `CompleteEnv::with_factory(...).complete()` as the first thing in `main` (`../vc-x1/src/main.rs:332`).
- And no, carapace can't be made compact in bash — `CARAPACE_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH=0` still emits full descriptions, so the one-per-line view is what bash gets, period.

So the honest bash-user comparison:

| | clap dynamic (vc-x1 style) | carapace spec (ours) |
|---|---|---|
| bash display | compact columns, no descriptions | one per line with descriptions |
| bench names | needs `ArgValueCandidates` added (same unstable feature) — clap only knows subcommands, and we have none | already live via exec-macro |
| context awareness | full (the binary parses the line) | good (spec grammar) |
| setup | `source <(COMPLETE=bash iiac-perf)` per app in rc | carapace once per machine + spec file (auto-installed by -8) |
| API stability | unstable feature, absorbed by us at compile time | all stable |
| non-bash shells | 5 shells; descriptions where the shell supports them | 11 shells, aligned description menus in zsh/fish/nushell |

One important note: vc-x1's pretty subcommand listing works because clap *knows* its subcommands. Our bench names are a free-form positional, so plain `CompleteEnv` would complete flags only — we'd add an `ArgValueCandidates` provider (part of the same unstable feature) returning `benches::names()` + `all`/`calibrate` to match what carapace already does.

These aren't exclusive: the binary can carry both, and whichever a user registers in their shell wins. My suggestion given your preference for the compact view: keep -7 as is (the carapace/static machinery stays for other shells and users), commit it, then make **-8 `feat: dynamic completion (CompleteEnv)`** — the vc-x1 pattern plus bench-name candidates, giving your bash exactly the vc-x1 experience — and push the `add-completion-yaml` self-install idea to **-9**, where it can install *either* integration (write the spec, or append the `COMPLETE=` line to the rc with your consent — solving the "I shouldn't have to edit anything" objection for dynamic too).

None are installed yet — all four are in the official repos, so no AUR needed this time. Here's the test-drive plan:

**Install (pick one or several):**
```
sudo pacman -S fish        # the "modern out-of-the-box" one
sudo pacman -S zsh         # the "bash, but nicer" one
sudo pacman -S nushell     # the radical rethink (tables/pipelines)
```

**Test-drive fish** (my pick for seeing completion at its best) — from your normal bash prompt:
```
fish                              # you're now in fish, temporarily
carapace _carapace fish | source  # hook carapace for this session only
iiac-perf <Tab>                   # bench menu
iiac-perf -<Tab>                  # flag menu — aligned two-column with descriptions
exit                              # back to bash, nothing changed
```

**Test-drive zsh:**
```
zsh
autoload -U compinit && compinit          # zsh's completion engine (one-time per session)
source <(carapace _carapace zsh)
iiac-perf -<Tab>                          # aligned "flag -- description" menu
exit
```

Nothing about your login shell changes until you decide you like one and run `chsh`. If you do, the carapace hook line moves into that shell's config file (`~/.config/fish/config.fish` or `~/.zshrc`) and your spec file works unchanged — that's the carapace payoff: same yaml, all shells.

**On your bash-scripts question — yes, exactly right.** A script starting with `#!/usr/bin/env bash` (or invoked as `bash foo.sh`) *always* executes under bash, no matter what shell you type commands in — the interactive shell and the script interpreter are completely independent. Your scripts, Makefiles, CI, everything keeps working untouched. What does *not* carry over automatically is your interactive environment: aliases, functions, prompt, and env exports live in `.bashrc`, and the new shell reads its own config instead. zsh is the gentle path there (`.zshrc` syntax is ~95% copy-paste from `.bashrc`); fish deliberately uses different syntax (`set -x VAR val` instead of `export VAR=val`), so its config is a rewrite — small for a typical rc, but real. A common cushion: keep bash as login shell and just launch `fish` when you want it, until the config feels settled.

Meanwhile the -7/-8 question from before is still open: keep -7 as is and re-ladder -8 to clap dynamic + -9 self-install — or does the shell experiment change your thinking first?

content.text:
Two of them, and conveniently they're the two most interesting:

- **fish** — yes, as of fish 4.0 (February 2025) it's fully Rust. The project spent ~2 years porting the entire C++ codebase; what `pacman -S fish` gives you today (4.x) is the Rust implementation.
- **nushell** — Rust from its first commit; it's one of the flagship large Rust applications.
- zsh is 30-year-old C, elvish is Go, xonsh is Python.

Honorable mentions from the Rust-shell world if you ever want to explore: **Ion** (the Redox OS shell) and **brush** (a bash-compatible shell reimplemented in Rust — interesting precisely because your muscle memory and `.bashrc` mostly keep working, though it's a younger project than the other two).

So the earlier recommendation stands with a Rust bonus: `fish` for the polished modern experience, `nushell` if you want to see the furthest departure (structured data flowing through pipelines instead of text) — both Rust, both fully supported by carapace, both test-drivable from bash with the commands from my last message.

Two things going on there — and note you're on the r5-7600x now, which matters for the test (more below).

**The fish 404s:** your local package database is stale — it still lists `fish-4.8.0-1`, but the mirrors have since replaced it with a newer release, so every mirror 404s on the old filename. The standard Arch fix:

```
sudo pacman -Syu
sudo pacman -S fish     # usually pulled in by -Syu's update anyway
```

(Full `-Syu`, not `-Sy fish` — refreshing the db and then installing a single package against otherwise-old libraries is the "partial upgrade" trap.) Nushell succeeded because the db entry for it happened to still match a file the mirrors carry.

**Trying nushell right now:** it uses an external-completer hook instead of a sourced script. For a throwaway session:

```

$env.config.completions.external.enable = true
$env.config.completions.external.completer = {|spans| carapace $spans.0 nushell ...$spans | from json }
iiac-perf <Tab>
```

content.text:
Good news on two fronts: your bash `PROMPT_COMMAND`/`PS1` aren't exported, so they don't leak into nushell — and nushell's config file is `~/.config/nushell/config.nu` (nu tells you the exact path via `$nu.config-path`). Everything session-y we did by hand goes there, prompt included.

A `config.nu` block that recreates your bash prompt's shape (`user@host timestamp:path`, `$` on the next line) plus the completer:

```nu
# Prompt: user@host ISO-timestamp:path, then "$ " on its own line
$env.PROMPT_COMMAND = {||
    let path = (pwd | str replace $nu.home-path "~")
    $"(ansi green)($env.USER)@(sys host | get hostname) (date now | format date '%y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%.3fZ')(ansi reset):(ansi light_blue_bold)($path)(ansi reset)"
}
$env.PROMPT_INDICATOR = "\n$ "
$env.PROMPT_COMMAND_RIGHT = ""      # drop the right-side clock if you don't want it

# Carapace external completions (what we set by hand in the session)
$env.config.completions.external.enable = true
$env.config.completions.external.completer = {|spans| carapace $spans.0 nushell ...$spans | from json }
```

Two notes worth having before you invest in that, though:

- Nushell's *default* prompt does show the cwd (green path + `>`), so if you saw none at all, something odd happened at first-run config creation — but with the block above it's moot.
- If you're going to keep shell-shopping (nu today, fish after `pacman -Syu`), consider **starship** (`pacman -S starship` — also Rust): it's a prompt engine that renders the *same* prompt — user, host, path, git/jj branch, timestamps — across bash, nushell, fish, and zsh from one `~/.config/starship.toml`. One-line hookup per shell, and your prompt stops being a reason to prefer any shell. Your git-branch-in-prompt bash setup suggests you'd want that piece in nu too, and starship gives it without hand-writing the git call in nu syntax.

And the standing reminder, gently: -7 is still parked awaiting your description approval and the -8/-9 re-ladder decision — the nushell experience (aligned descriptions, no bash renderer fight) may have just made the "add clap dynamic for bash's sake" step feel less necessary.

content.text:
Option A locked in — conveniently the ladder already reads that way (-8 `feat: completion self-install command`, then close-out), so no edit needed; I'll add the CompleteEnv backlog idea to todo.md as part of -8's commit. Still holding the -7 push until you say go.

Now the languages — both shells deliberately abandoned POSIX, in different directions:

**fish** speaks its own language, best described as "shell, but with the footguns removed." It's still a command language — you type commands and pipe text — but: every variable is a list (no word-splitting/quoting hell — `$files` with spaces just works), assignment is `set name value`, blocks end with `end` instead of `fi`/`done`/`esac`, functions are `function greet ... end`, command substitution is `(cmd)` (and `$(cmd)` also works in 4.x). Example:

```fish
function backup
    for f in *.rs
        cp $f $f.bak
    end
end
```

The fish community's own convention is: fish for interactive use and small config functions, bash/POSIX for portable scripts — which fits your `#!/usr/bin/env bash` reality perfectly.

**nushell** is the bigger leap: a genuine typed, structured-data language where pipelines carry *tables and records*, not text. `ls` returns a table with typed columns (filesize, datetime); you filter and transform it like a dataframe. Functions have typed signatures, closures are first-class (`{|spans| ...}` from our completer hook is one), there are modules, real error handling, and native JSON/TOML/YAML/CSV conversion. Example — "largest three .rs files as a table":

```nu
ls src/*.rs | sort-by size --reverse | first 3 | select name size
```

The closest ancestor is PowerShell's object pipeline, re-imagined with Rust-flavored syntax. Nu scripts (`.nu`) are real programs — our `vc-x1`-style tooling could genuinely be written in it — with the caveat that the language still makes breaking changes between releases, so scripts need occasional maintenance in a way bash never does.

The plain version: fish is bash's job done cleaner — same kind of language, fewer traps, not portable. Nushell is a different species — data flows as tables you query, closer to a programming language wearing a shell costume. Neither replaces your bash scripts; both replace only your typing.
